questions.question: Explain Kafka producer acknowledgments and when you would use each setting in production.
questions.direct_answer: Kafka producers have three ack modes: acks=0 (fire-and-forget, no confirmation), acks=1 (leader partition confirms, replicas may lag), and acks=all (all in-sync replicas confirm before returning). For financial transactions or critical data, use acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2. For high-throughput metrics pipelines where occasional loss is acceptable, acks=0 maximizes throughput.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the durability vs throughput trade-off, not just what each setting means
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying acks=all is always the right answer — it kills throughput for use cases like log aggregation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention min.insync.replicas and explain a real scenario where you chose a specific ack setting and why

sections.title: The Durability vs Throughput Trade-off
sections.content:
Every Kafka producer send is a bet: how much latency are you willing to pay for durability? The `acks` setting controls how many brokers must confirm they've written your record before the producer considers it "sent." Three modes exist — `acks=0` (fire and forget), `acks=1` (leader confirms), and `acks=all` (all in-sync replicas confirm). Choosing the wrong one means either losing critical financial data or adding unnecessary latency to a metrics pipeline that doesn't need it.

The real subtlety isn't the ack mode itself — it's how `acks` interacts with `min.insync.replicas`, `retries`, and idempotence. Getting acks=all right requires configuring all four together.

sections.title: The Three Ack Modes Explained
sections.content:
**acks=0 (Fire and Forget)** — The producer sends the record and moves on immediately. No confirmation from any broker. The returned offset is -1 (meaningless). If the broker is down, the record is silently lost. Throughput is 2-3x higher than acks=1 because there's zero round-trip wait. Use for: metrics pipelines, click-stream analytics, sensor telemetry — anywhere losing a few events per million is acceptable.

**acks=1 (Leader Acknowledges)** — The partition leader writes the record to its local log and sends back confirmation. The producer knows the record reached at least one broker. The risk: if the leader crashes after acknowledging but *before* replicating to followers, that record is gone when a new leader is elected. Use for: application logs, non-critical notifications, audit trails where very rare loss (leader crash during replication lag) is tolerable.

**acks=all / acks=-1 (All In-Sync Replicas)** — The leader waits until every replica in the ISR (in-sync replica set) has written the record, then acknowledges. As long as any ISR member survives, your data is safe. This is the only mode suitable for financial transactions, payment events, or any data you cannot afford to lose.

sections.title: min.insync.replicas: The Hidden Requirement
sections.content:
`acks=all` alone is **not enough**. By default, `min.insync.replicas=1` — meaning a single replica (the leader itself) satisfies the "all" requirement. This defeats the entire purpose.

The production configuration:

```
replication.factor = 3          // 3 copies of every partition
min.insync.replicas = 2         // at least 2 must be in sync
acks = all                      // wait for all ISR members
```

With this setup: if one broker is down, two remain in sync — writes proceed normally. If two brokers are down, only one is left (below min.insync.replicas), and the producer gets `NotEnoughReplicasException` — the system refuses to accept data it can't safely replicate. This is the correct behavior: **failing loudly is better than silently losing data**.

The math: with `replication.factor=3` and `min.insync.replicas=2`, you can tolerate exactly one broker failure while maintaining full durability guarantees.

sections.title: Idempotent Producers and Exactly-Once Delivery
Key Points
sections.content:
- **acks=0** sends without waiting — maximum throughput, zero durability. Good for metrics, bad for payments. Returned offset is -1
- **acks=1** waits for the leader — data survives unless the leader crashes before replicating. Covers 95% of non-critical use cases
- **acks=all** waits for all ISR members — only mode for critical data. Must pair with `min.insync.replicas=2` or the "all" is meaningless (default is 1)
- **Idempotent producer** (`enable.idempotence=true`) prevents duplicates from retries via PID + sequence number. Default since Kafka 3.0 — no reason to disable it
- **The production formula**: `replication.factor=3` + `min.insync.replicas=2` + `acks=all` + `enable.idempotence=true` = durable, deduplicated, can tolerate 1 broker failure

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kafka producer acks are about the **durability vs throughput trade-off**. `acks=0` is fire and forget — maximum throughput but zero guarantee the broker even received the record. `acks=1` means the partition leader confirms the write, which covers most cases, but if the leader crashes before replicating you lose that record. `acks=all` waits for every in-sync replica to confirm — this is the only mode I'd use for anything financial.

The critical detail most people miss is that `acks=all` alone isn't enough. You need `min.insync.replicas=2` on the topic, otherwise "all" can be satisfied by just the leader. The production setup I use is `replication.factor=3`, `min.insync.replicas=2`, `acks=all`, plus `enable.idempotence=true` to prevent duplicates from retries. That gives you durable, deduplicated writes that tolerate one broker failure.

For a metrics pipeline I'd use `acks=0` — losing a few data points per million doesn't matter, and you get 2-3x the throughput.

questions.question: How do Kafka consumer groups work and what happens during a rebalance?
questions.direct_answer: A consumer group is a set of consumers sharing the work of consuming a topic. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group at any time, enabling horizontal scaling. A rebalance is triggered when consumers join/leave/crash or partitions change — during it, all consumption pauses and partitions are reassigned. In production, rebalances are painful because they cause processing gaps and can cause duplicate processing if offsets aren't committed before the rebalance completes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the partition-consumer relationship and have seen the practical pain of rebalances in production
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking more consumers always means more parallelism — you can't have more consumers than partitions effectively
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention cooperative rebalancing (Kafka 2.4+) and how it eliminates the stop-the-world problem

sections.title: Partition Assignment and the Consumer Group Protocol
sections.content:
A Kafka **consumer group** is a set of consumers that cooperatively read from a topic by dividing its partitions among themselves. The fundamental rule: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer within a group at any time. This guarantees that records within a partition are processed by a single consumer in order.

The group coordinator (a Kafka broker) manages membership and partition assignment. When the group membership changes — a consumer joins, leaves, or is considered dead — the coordinator triggers a **rebalance** to redistribute partitions. Rebalances are necessary but painful: they pause consumption and can cause duplicate processing if offsets aren't committed cleanly.

sections.title: How Partition Assignment Works
sections.content:
If a topic has 12 partitions and a consumer group has 3 consumers, each consumer gets 4 partitions. Add a 4th consumer → each gets 3. Add a 13th consumer → one sits idle because you can't split a partition between consumers. **Partition count is the parallelism ceiling.**

Two consumer groups reading the same topic are completely independent — each group gets ALL partitions. This is the broadcast pattern: `group-A` and `group-B` both see every record. Within each group, partitions are divided.

The assignment strategy determines which consumer gets which partitions:
- **RangeAssignor** (old default): assigns contiguous ranges. Consumer 0 gets partitions 0-3, consumer 1 gets 4-7. Simple but uneven across multiple topics
- **RoundRobinAssignor**: distributes partitions round-robin. More even but less predictable
- **StickyAssignor**: tries to keep the same assignment after rebalance, minimizing partition movement
- **CooperativeStickyAssignor** (recommended): same as sticky but with cooperative rebalancing — the critical upgrade

sections.title: Rebalancing: The Eager vs Cooperative Problem
sections.content:
**Eager rebalancing (old default)** is stop-the-world. When triggered, ALL consumers revoke ALL their partitions simultaneously, then the coordinator reassigns everything from scratch. If you have 100 partitions across 10 consumers and one consumer dies, all 90 remaining assigned partitions stop being consumed — not just the 10 that need redistribution. Consumption pauses for seconds to minutes depending on group size.

**What triggers a rebalance:**
- Consumer joins (new instance or restart)
- Consumer leaves (clean shutdown via `consumer.close()`)
- Consumer crashes (missed heartbeat — `session.timeout.ms` exceeded)
- Processing takes too long (`max.poll.interval.ms` exceeded between `poll()` calls)
- Partitions added to the topic

**Cooperative rebalancing (Kafka 2.4+)** is incremental. Only the partitions that need to move are revoked. Consumers that keep their partitions continue processing uninterrupted. A consumer dying with 10 partitions causes only those 10 to be redistributed — the other 90 continue normally.

```java
// Enable cooperative rebalancing — one config change, massive impact
props.put(ConsumerConfig.PARTITION_ASSIGNMENT_STRATEGY_CONFIG,
    CooperativeStickyAssignor.class.getName());
```

sections.title: Duplicate Processing and Offset Management
Key Points
sections.content:
- **One partition = one consumer per group** — partition count is the parallelism ceiling. More consumers than partitions means idle consumers
- **Rebalance pauses all consumption** in eager mode. Switch to `CooperativeStickyAssignor` to make rebalances incremental (only moved partitions stop)
- **session.timeout.ms** is heartbeat-based (broker declares consumer dead). **max.poll.interval.ms** is processing-based (consumer taking too long between polls). Tune both for your workload
- **Disable auto-commit** (`enable.auto.commit=false`) and commit manually after processing to prevent data loss during rebalances
- **Two groups on the same topic** = broadcast — each group independently gets all partitions. Within a group, partitions are divided (competing consumers pattern)

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A consumer group is a set of consumers that **divide a topic's partitions** among themselves. The core rule: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group. So 12 partitions and 3 consumers means each gets 4. You can't have more active consumers than partitions — extras sit idle.

A **rebalance** happens when the group membership changes — a consumer joins, leaves, crashes, or takes too long to process. In the old eager mode, rebalancing is stop-the-world: all consumers drop all partitions and get them reassigned from scratch. Even if only one consumer died, everyone pauses. **Cooperative rebalancing** in Kafka 2.4+ fixes this — only the partitions that need to move are revoked, everything else keeps processing.

The production danger is **duplicate processing**. If a consumer processes records but hasn't committed the offset when a rebalance hits, the new consumer assigned that partition re-processes those records. The fix is disabling auto-commit and committing manually after processing — you get at-least-once semantics, which means your downstream processing should be idempotent.

questions.question: How does Kafka partitioning work and how do you ensure message ordering?
questions.direct_answer: Kafka maintains strict ordering only within a single partition. Messages with the same key always go to the same partition (via hash of the key mod num_partitions), guaranteeing order per key. For global ordering across all messages, you need exactly one partition — which eliminates parallelism entirely. In practice, you design your key to be the unit of ordering you care about: user_id for user events, order_id for payment events.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the ordering guarantee boundary and can design keys for real use cases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Kafka guarantees global ordering across partitions — it does not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the trade-off: more partitions = more parallelism but potentially out-of-order processing for unkeyed messages; show you've thought about key design for your domain

sections.title: Ordering Guarantees: Per-Partition, Not Per-Topic
sections.content:
Kafka guarantees strict ordering **within a single partition** — records are appended in order and consumed in order. Across partitions, there is **no ordering guarantee**. This is the fundamental constraint that drives all Kafka key design decisions.

The partition a record goes to is determined by its **key**. Same key → same partition → ordered processing. No key → round-robin distribution → no ordering. This means your key design IS your ordering strategy.

sections.title: The Partitioning Algorithm and Key Design
sections.content:
By default, Kafka uses `murmur2(key) % numPartitions` to assign records to partitions. This is deterministic — the same key always maps to the same partition, as long as the partition count doesn't change.

Key design for real systems:

```
User events      → key = user_id     (all events for a user are ordered)
Payment events   → key = order_id    (payment state transitions are ordered)
IoT sensors      → key = device_id   (sensor readings arrive in sequence)
Database CDC     → key = table:pk    (row-level changes stay ordered)
```

**No key** = round-robin (older clients) or sticky partitioning (Kafka 2.4+ — batches go to the same partition for efficiency, then rotate). Either way, no ordering guarantee.

The choice of key is a design decision that directly affects:
- **Ordering**: only same-key records are ordered
- **Parallelism**: one key can only be processed by one consumer at a time
- **Load balance**: if one key generates 80% of traffic, one partition gets 80% of load (the hot partition problem)

sections.title: The Partition Count Change Problem
sections.content:
Adding partitions to a topic **breaks existing key-to-partition mappings**. A key that mapped to partition 2 with 6 partitions might map to partition 7 with 12 partitions. For consumers replaying from the beginning, events for the same key will appear in two different partitions — ordering is broken across the boundary.

Best practices:
- **Over-provision partitions upfront** — 50-100 partitions for a medium-scale topic is common. You can always have more partitions than consumers (extras queue up), but adding partitions later is painful
- **Removing partitions is impossible** without recreating the topic
- If you must add partitions, accept that historical key mappings are broken. New records will be correctly partitioned; old ones won't migrate
- For topics where ordering is critical across key-space changes, consider using a custom partitioner with a lookup table rather than hash-based assignment

sections.title: Hot Partitions and Custom Partitioners
sections.content:
The **hot partition problem** occurs when one key generates disproportionate traffic. In a social media platform, a celebrity user's `user_id` might produce 1000x more events than a regular user — that single partition becomes the bottleneck.

Solutions:
- **Compound keys**: `user_id + event_type` — spreads a single user's events across partitions by type. You lose per-user ordering across event types but gain load balance
- **Custom partitioner**: implement `Partitioner` interface to route hot keys across multiple partitions intentionally. Your consumer must handle out-of-order processing for those keys
- **Accept the imbalance**: if the hot partition is still within throughput limits, it's simpler to leave it alone

For **global ordering** (all messages in sequence across the entire topic), use exactly one partition. This eliminates parallelism entirely — throughput is limited to a single consumer. Only viable for low-volume topics like configuration changes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Ordering is per-partition only** — Kafka makes zero ordering guarantees across partitions. Design your key to match your ordering needs
- **Same key = same partition** via `murmur2(key) % numPartitions`. Changing partition count breaks this mapping for existing data
- **Over-provision partitions** (50-100 for medium topics) because adding partitions is disruptive and removing them is impossible
- **Hot partition problem**: one key with 80% of traffic → one partition with 80% of load. Fix with compound keys or custom partitioners
- **Global ordering requires 1 partition** — eliminates parallelism. Only use for low-volume control topics

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kafka guarantees ordering **within a partition**, not across partitions. Think of partitions as lanes on a highway — cars in the same lane arrive in order, but cars in different lanes don't. The message **key** determines the lane: `murmur2(key) % numPartitions` is the default algorithm, so the same key always goes to the same partition.

This means key design is the critical decision. For a payment system I'd use `order_id` as the key — all state transitions for one order are ordered. For user events, `user_id`. The key has to match whatever entity needs ordered processing.

The trap is **changing partition count**. If you go from 6 to 12 partitions, the hash mapping changes and a key that was in partition 2 might now go to partition 7. Historical data doesn't migrate. That's why you over-provision upfront — 50-100 partitions is common even for moderate throughput topics.

If you need global ordering across ALL messages, you need exactly one partition — but that means exactly one consumer, which kills parallelism. In practice, per-key ordering is almost always sufficient.

questions.question: Explain Kafka's exactly-once semantics and how you would implement it.
questions.direct_answer: Kafka achieves exactly-once semantics (EOS) through three layered guarantees: idempotent producers (prevent duplicates from retries), transactional APIs (atomic write across multiple partitions), and transactional consumers (read-process-write atomically). EOS has real overhead — 20-30% throughput reduction — so only use it where duplicates are genuinely unacceptable, like financial transactions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the full EOS stack, not just that it exists, and understand when the overhead is worth it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking acks=all alone gives exactly-once — it gives at-least-once with durability
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between producer-side EOS (idempotent producer) and end-to-end EOS (transactions), and name the stream processing frameworks that use it under the hood

sections.title: Three Layers of Exactly-Once
sections.content:
Exactly-once semantics (EOS) in Kafka is not a single feature — it's three layered guarantees working together. **Layer 1**: idempotent producers (prevent duplicates from retries). **Layer 2**: transactional APIs (atomic writes across multiple partitions). **Layer 3**: transactional consumers (`read_committed` isolation). Each layer builds on the previous one.

EOS has real cost — 20-30% throughput reduction. Use it only where duplicates are genuinely unacceptable: financial transactions, inventory updates, billing events. For analytics or logging, at-least-once with idempotent downstream processing is simpler and faster.

sections.title: Layer 1: Idempotent Producer — Deduplicate Retries
sections.content:
Enable with `enable.idempotence=true` (default since Kafka 3.0). The broker assigns a **Producer ID (PID)** and tracks the **sequence number** per partition. If the producer retries a send (network timeout, broker restart), the broker recognizes the duplicate via PID + sequence and returns success without writing a second copy.

Without idempotence, this happens: producer sends record → broker writes it → acknowledgment lost in transit → producer retries → broker writes a second copy. With idempotence: the retry is detected and discarded.

```java
Properties props = new Properties();
props.put(ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG, true); // PID + sequence tracking
props.put(ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG, "all");              // required for idempotence
props.put(ProducerConfig.RETRIES_CONFIG, Integer.MAX_VALUE); // retry until success
// max.in.flight.requests.per.connection can be up to 5 with idempotence
// (the broker reorders out-of-sequence requests correctly)
```

Idempotent producers give you **exactly-once from producer to broker** with negligible overhead. This should be on for every producer.

sections.title: Layer 2: Transactional Producer — Atomic Multi-Partition Writes
Layer 3: The Full Read-Process-Write Pattern
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Idempotent producer** (Layer 1) deduplicates retries via PID + sequence number. Negligible overhead — should be default for all producers
- **Transactional producer** (Layer 2) makes multi-partition writes atomic. Requires a stable `transactional.id` per application instance for zombie fencing
- **read_committed consumers** (Layer 3) only see committed transaction output. Without this, consumers see uncommitted records — defeating EOS
- **sendOffsetsToTransaction** is the key method — it atomically commits consumer offsets and producer output in one transaction
- **20-30% throughput overhead** is real. Only use EOS where duplicates genuinely matter (payments, inventory). For analytics, at-least-once + idempotent processing is simpler

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Exactly-once in Kafka is built in three layers. The first is the **idempotent producer** — it assigns a sequence number to each record so the broker can detect and discard retries. This prevents duplicates from producer to broker with almost zero overhead.

The second layer is the **transactional API**. You call `beginTransaction()`, send to multiple partitions, then `commitTransaction()` — either all records commit or none do. The broker holds them in pending state until commit. If the producer crashes, pending transactions are aborted.

The third layer ties it together: the **read-process-write pattern**. You consume records, process them, produce output, and commit consumer offsets all in one atomic transaction via `sendOffsetsToTransaction()`. If the process crashes mid-way, both the output and the offsets are rolled back — so on recovery, records are re-read and reprocessed without duplicates.

The practical consideration: EOS costs **20-30% throughput**. I'd only use it for financial transactions or inventory updates. For analytics, at-least-once with idempotent downstream processing is simpler and faster. Kafka Streams gives you EOS essentially for free if you're using it.

questions.question: What is the difference between Kafka log retention and log compaction? When would you use each?
questions.direct_answer: Log retention deletes old records after a time period (log.retention.hours, default 7 days) or size limit — old history is gone. Log compaction keeps only the latest record per key indefinitely, deleting older records with the same key but preserving the most recent state. Use retention for event streams where you only care about recent events. Use compaction for state/changelog topics where you need the current value per key regardless of age — like a database change log or user preferences topic.

sections.title: Two Cleanup Strategies for Different Use Cases
sections.content:
Kafka stores records in an append-only log on disk. Without cleanup, the log grows forever. Two strategies manage this: **retention** (delete old records after a time/size limit) and **compaction** (keep only the latest record per key, indefinitely). They answer different questions: retention answers "what happened recently?" and compaction answers "what is the current state?"

You set the strategy per-topic with `cleanup.policy` — and you can even combine both.

sections.title: Log Retention: Time-Based or Size-Based Deletion
sections.content:
**`cleanup.policy=delete`** (the default). Kafka deletes log segments older than `log.retention.hours` (default: 168 hours / 7 days) or when the total log exceeds `log.retention.bytes`. Old data is gone — no replay possible.

Deletion happens at the **segment** level, not individual records. A segment is a chunk of the log (default 1GB or 7 days, whichever comes first). When the oldest segment passes the retention threshold, the entire segment is deleted.

Use retention for **event streams** where you only care about recent data:
- Application logs (who needs 6-month-old logs in Kafka?)
- Click-stream analytics (recent trends, not 2019 data)
- Metrics pipelines (historical data lives in Prometheus/Grafana, not Kafka)
- Temporary processing queues (data consumed and done)

sections.title: Log Compaction: Keep Latest State Per Key
sections.content:
**`cleanup.policy=compact`**. A background thread periodically scans the log and removes older records that share a key with a newer record. The result: the topic contains exactly one record per key — the most recent one.

Records with a **null value** are called **tombstones** — they signal that a key should be considered deleted. Compaction eventually removes tombstones too (after `delete.retention.ms`, default 24 hours).

Use compaction for **state/changelog topics** where you need current state regardless of age:
- Database CDC (Change Data Capture) — new consumers replay just current state, not every historical update
- User profile/preferences — current settings, not the full change history
- Kafka Streams changelog topics — state store backup and recovery
- Service configuration — current config per service key

The compaction guarantee: at least the **latest value per key** is always retained. Compaction runs in the background, so there's a lag — older duplicates exist temporarily until the compaction thread processes them.

sections.title: Combining Both and Practical Configuration
sections.content:
**`cleanup.policy=compact,delete`** — compaction removes superseded keys, AND time-based retention removes old tombstones and records for deleted keys. This prevents tombstone accumulation in long-lived compacted topics.

```
# Pure retention (event stream)
cleanup.policy=delete
retention.ms=604800000          # 7 days

# Pure compaction (state topic)
cleanup.policy=compact
min.compaction.lag.ms=0         # compact immediately
delete.retention.ms=86400000    # keep tombstones for 24h

# Combined (state topic with tombstone cleanup)
cleanup.policy=compact,delete
retention.ms=2592000000         # delete records older than 30 days
min.compaction.lag.ms=3600000   # don't compact records less than 1 hour old
```

Practical note: a new consumer group subscribing to a compacted topic gets the compacted state — it doesn't replay the original full history. This is what makes compacted topics useful as lightweight databases: any new service can "bootstrap" its state by consuming the compacted topic from the beginning.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Retention** (`cleanup.policy=delete`) deletes old segments by time or size — simple, predictable, data is gone permanently
- **Compaction** (`cleanup.policy=compact`) keeps only the latest record per key — acts like a key-value store that any new consumer can bootstrap from
- **Tombstones** (null value) mark a key as deleted in compacted topics. They're kept for `delete.retention.ms` (default 24h) so consumers have time to see the deletion
- **Combine both** (`compact,delete`) to compact keys AND clean up old tombstones — prevents unbounded tombstone growth
- **Compaction is not instant** — there's a lag between a new record arriving and the old one being removed. Don't rely on compaction for real-time deduplication

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Retention is like a **news feed** — you keep recent articles and delete old ones after a week. Compaction is like a **database snapshot** — you keep the latest version of every record, forever, regardless of when it was written.

**Retention** (`cleanup.policy=delete`) is the default. Records are deleted when the log segment is older than `log.retention.hours` or bigger than `log.retention.bytes`. Use it for event streams where only recent data matters: logs, metrics, click-streams.

**Compaction** (`cleanup.policy=compact`) keeps only the most recent record per key. A background thread removes older duplicates. The key use case is CDC or changelog topics — a new service that spins up can consume the compacted topic from the beginning and get the current state of every entity without replaying years of updates.

You can also **combine both** — `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` — which compacts keys and also removes old tombstones. This is what I use for long-lived state topics to prevent tombstones from accumulating indefinitely.
